utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We are going to resume our work. Good morning to the technical booth and to the interpreters. I hope that this is going to be our last week when it comes to tendering evidence in this case. There is a motion filed by the Defence for the submission of evidence in the Blaskic case. We can give an oral ruling, and we will have a written decision later. The ruling issued by this Trial Chamber is as follows: This Trial Chamber is going to order that public elements of the testimony by Admiral Domazet be tendered into evidence and that other elements and the video recording be tendered as well, as they were presented in the Blaskic case. This is an oral ruling, but we are going to put this into writing, and this will be published in this way. I thought it was relevant for both parties to be informed of our position as just stated. I think we can now start with our work. Mr. Mikulicic, I think it is now your turn to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. First of all, I wish you good morning, as well as my learned colleagues a very good morning. We are reaching the end of the proceedings and the presenting of evidence in this case. The Defence would like to call its last witness with regard to the facts, and we wish to oppose some of the testimonies made by the Prosecution witnesses. We now call Witness Blazan Blazevic to the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Mikulicic, but did you not ask for protective measures regarding this witness? Is he going to be protected or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for this witness, the Defence has not called for protective measures, but it asks for protective measures for two witnesses which it will be examining with regard to the character of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Please have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Can you hear me? I, the Judge, am talking to you. Good morning, sir. I am going to ask you to read out the solemn declaration which the usher is just handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: How do you feel? Are you feeling comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm a little nervous. I've never been to a court before, so I am a little nervous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That's quite natural, but you will be treated fairly. Don't you worry. Mr. Mikulicic is going to put questions to you, and we'll start with that. Go ahead, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Blazevic. As the Judge has just stated, my name is Goran Mikulicic, the Defence counsel. I'm going to ask you several questions, and I would like to ask you to answer them to the best of your recollection. When I ask my questions and when you give your replies, please take into account the fact that we must speak slowly and to make brief pauses between sentences to facilitate the work of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, would you please tell us when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 24th of May, 1949 in the municipality of Busovaca in the village of Donje Polje, which is where I now live.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, would you tell us what you are by way of ethnicity and religion?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I am a Christian, a Roman Catholic and a believer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Which is your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, what are you by profession? What schools have you completed?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Eight years of primary school, and I worked in the steelworks before the war for 15 years, up to the war, that is. After the war, I am unemployed. I have been unemployed and I'm at home. I have some livestock. I have some land, and I work privately as a farmer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that you worked in the steelworks. Do you mean the steelworks in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the steelworks in Zenica as a crane operator, skilled crane operator, 15 years up until the war, but there is no employment for Croats in Zenica anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Blazevic, are you married?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm married. I had six children. Now I have five. One of my children was killed during the war. He was my son, a 17-year-old. Two others were wounded at home tending to the cattle in the fields. One was seriously wounded, and he is a 60 per cent invalid. He was shelled in the stomach. The other one is a 30 per cent invalid. I have two more sons, that is to say, three sons and two daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you do military service in the former JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, for 18 months. I spent 6 months in Krizevci, in Croatia, and the rest of the time I spent in Ptuj, in Slovenia, as a radio telephonist operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether you had any military training in the army and any rank?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was a regular soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, upon your return from the army, did you become part of the reservist formations of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and every other year I joined up as a reservist for a period. I spent some time at Kaonik near Sarajevo. I spent some 10 to 15 days around Bosnia, that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're talking about the military training that you were called to attend as a reservist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, you mentioned that, during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, you lost a son and that two other sons were wounded. Did you participate in some way in the events in Bosnia-Herzegovina, beginning from 1991 onwards?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a volunteer in the war at the outset of the war in Croatia. First of all, it began in Slovenia, of course, and then it moved to Croatia. The Yugoslav People's Army was fortifying their lines in Bosnia at Vlasici, Jajce, and along the hills there. They had positioned their heavy artillery and guns. I became a member of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade, and then we went up to the frontlines on guard there. I was in Jajce for ten days. I was in Podvlasce for 10 to 15 days. Then we would have night duty, night watch, at home. Two or three of us would do this duty to prevent anybody storming the village during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Blazevic, you talked about the part of the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was waged against the Yugoslav People's Army and the Serbian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were together with the Muslims. The Muslims and Croats were together. We mounted the lines against the Serbs, against the Chetniks. Up until then, there was no conflict between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say, Mr. Blazevic, that, at the beginning, you had joint forces with persons of the Muslim faith against the Serbian army. What happened then afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, afterwards, the Muslim army and the Croatian army separated, because the Muslim villages, for the most part, were in the hilly areas, whereas us Croats were below, like, Vitez, Kiseljak, Busovaca, in the plains. At that time, digging was going on in the Muslim parts of the hills. Trenches were being dug. My children tended to the livestock. I have 100 dulums of land, and my children told me that they were being expelled from our own fields by the Muslims, and they started digging trenches on my land. So on one occasion, I went to ask them what they were doing. I said, "What are you doing?" And they said, "Well, we are doing this against the Chetniks, against the Serbs," and there were no Serbs there. The Serbs were 100 kilometres away. On that occasion, we saw that, in fact, something was being prepared, probably against us Croats, so we had night watches in the villages to safeguard our houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I have understood you correctly, Mr. Blazevic, you know about this situation because it was on your own land, on your own property, that the members of the Muslim Bosniak nation dug trenches?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They dug trenches in the hills, and, quite normally, I informed my superiors in Busovaca of what I had seen. He said, "Well, that's none of your business. It's not your affair. There are others who will think about that." So I just kept silent after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Blazevic, as far as you can recall, when did these events take place? What year was this?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It was probably, I don't remember exactly, and I seem to have lost my memory rather a lot, but I think it was 1993 or thereabouts, the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what happened at the end of January and the beginning of February 1993 in the Busovaca region where you lived? Was there any conflict?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: In the spring, in the early spring, I don't remember the exact date, our young men passed by Busovaca towards Kiseljak. There was a car, a tam, and there were five or six soldiers in Kacuni, the Croatian soldiers in Kacuni, where the Muslims were. They fired from a Zolja, a hand-held rocket launcher. They attacked the car. I think one or two died on the occasion. I think Miljenko Perkovic was one of them. I don't remember his name. The other was wounded. They took the vehicle and fled to the wood. They came to Kiseljak two or three months later, I believe, and on that occasion, we started digging as well around our own houses, and there was a dugout right by my own house. On the last day, they attacked us. It was an organised attack. Five of our young men in my vicinity were killed on that occasion. That's how it began, in that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That means, Mr. Blazevic, that you recall that these conflicts between the Croats and Muslims, in fact, started with the incident in Kacuni when two HVO soldiers were killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That was the main incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before that, there weren't any. Two days later, an attack was launched on Busovaca and on your own village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Two days later, I think it was the 26th of January, and I don't remember exactly, but that's when we were attacked by them. They formed three lines. It was cold. There were a lot of soldiers, and there were Muslims dressed in white. They launched a massive attack. We had to move our lines a little, but that is how it began between the Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where were you at that time? Which line were you manning at that time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Right by my house. We had made a sort of sand fortification, and we used sand and manure, because I had some manure. We made these dugouts, and that is where I was when they launched their attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're talking about these events dating back to January 1993. Tell me, please, how long did the attack last? How long did these hostilities last; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I don't mean just that particular day, but how long did it last? How many days? How many weeks?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was an ongoing process. We entrenched and they attacked. They were up above us. We were down below. We had our trenches, our dugouts, and we began digging. We were assisted in this digging by the work platoon, and we did this digging at night. That was the only time we could do it. There was shooting all the time. This line by my house was a permanent line, whereas the others shifted slightly towards the town of Busovaca itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. Mr. Blazevic, you mentioned that you had some assistance, that you soldiers defending the frontline were given some help in digging trenches and dugouts. You mentioned some work platoons. Could you explain that and describe that to us, please? Who were these people who helped you? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember one night, there were some 20 people that came to help us. There were Muslims as well and Croats, and they came to dig the trenches. I recognised there three Muslims, my neighbours, and I invited them into my house. I asked them whether they were hungry, and they said, "Well, yes, we could have a bite to eat. Thank you." They went into the house. We had some coffee. They had something to eat, what there was. They had a bath, and they went out to continue digging up till dawn when the Military Police came to take these people back, and probably they were the prisoners, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, you mentioned that they were taken away by the Military Police. Who brought them to your house to dig the trenches? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It was the Military Police again, and they deployed them there and told us to stand guard there. There were also some guards and the combatants who were guarding that particular line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, the Bosnian nationals of Muslim ethnic origin, where were they brought from by the Military Police?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I learned that they had been brought to prison, but why that was so, I would not know. I know that the Military Police brought them to dig those trenches, dugouts, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know which prison that was, as you call?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the prison was the one in Kaonik. There were no other prisons there. The Military Police was also quartered there, and they brought them and took them away, I mean, to work and from work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that you also knew personally some of those men, and some of them you invited into your house, and the like. Do you remember certain names?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I do. I think Hamdo Ibrilic and two youngish men. There were two or three young men with us who sat in my house, had coffee, had some food, took a bath, and the like.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, will you please tell us, apart from those Muslims, the Bosniaks, were there also some other men, Croats, who were brought to dig, or were there only Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: There were Croats and there were Muslims, regardless -- and there was also a work platoon, and they just worked, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, those Croats who also worked there, who were those people?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: The Croats, those who worked there, were mostly men who were not able-bodied, that is, who were too old for the army, the elderly, and yet they were there because they had to help in some way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To your mind, Mr. Blazevic, why did the soldiers, who were defending the line, need all this help in digging trenches? Were you sufficient enough to do it or not?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, we were not. We were not too many, I mean, the soldiers, and we were not prepared for the war, so not a single dugout was really dug until they attacked us. Then the time was such that for 15 days we would not take off our boots, and we were simply exhausted and asked for some help, some assistance. So let them dig trenches, if nothing else. There were people who came and merely stood and watched when it would start, so we simply needed some help.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. I understand. Mr. Blazevic, you said that those people came to help, that they were being brought by the Military Police, and that there were military sentry watching them as they dug those trenches; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember if there were any incidents or whether any of those men who dug trenches were wounded or hurt or whatever; do you remember anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No. No, nothing like that happened. Nobody was to blame for this for it just happened, and they were doing their job. We were there. But it was not safe at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, in that situation, when people were brought to the defence line to help with the fortification and digging of trenches, who was their superior? Who ordered them? Who ordered them to dig here or there, stop digging, and so on and so forth? Who issued orders?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Those men who were up on the line. They knew where it was necessary, when we had to dig, and so they told them to dig here and wherever, and they always obeyed without any problem, both Croats and Muslims equally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say "we," I mean, what does it mean, "we"?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: The combatants, we who were positioned on the line. We were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I expect that on that segment of the line which you, the combatants, held, there was also a commander too?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was the commander, Dragan Akrap, called Mance. He was the commander of the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski, if I remember it well, the 1st Battalion of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So Mance, as you call him, he was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: He was the commander of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that he commanded -- he was the superior of that work unit which was attached to you to help?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't know with certainty, but I guess that in all likelihood he was because they were digging trenches there where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, you mentioned that these people, those Muslims from Kaonik, had been brought by the Military Police to the place where they were to dig. Did the Military Police also bring Croats, that is, Croat civilians, also to dig trenches, or did they come in some other manner?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, they came together, both the Croats and Muslims, and the Military Police would always bring them there and then take them back; and the combatants, those who were on the line, they stood watch, and these people went back to the barracks over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. So far, we talked about the events in 1993, that is, sometime in January and February, that is, at the time of the first Muslim-Croat conflict in the Lasva Valley. Could you now please try to remember when the second conflict happened because, meanwhile, there was a truce of a kind or something?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Up to the first conflict, the cease-fire was signed, and if I recall properly, it was in April, I think towards the end of April. I wouldn't know the date exactly. Fifteenth, 16th -- no, I wouldn't know. But at any rate, a truce was signed. So we were sitting by the dugout -- the dugouts were very close, I mean ours and the Muslim ones -- and one morning, I remember that very well, the Muslims -- of course, we knew each other very well because we were neighbours because -- and one of them, especially because we worked together at the steelworks and commuted by bus every morning, and called "Dugonja," that was my nickname, "Come and have a cup of coffee."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. I'm sorry. Will you please explain once again who was it that called to you?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Muslims. They were some 100, 200 metres away. They were very close.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about members of the B and H army?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. They called me, they called to me, called to me, "Dugonja, come and have a cup of coffee with us." There was no fire at the time. But I answered, "No, I will not. Why don't you come over to me?" Then a pause and then again they called to me, "Come and have a cup of coffee with us." "I won't." As a matter of fact, I did not dare. "Why don't you come over to me?" "Here we come."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. May we clarify this thing? This is happening at a time when you are in a dugout on the defence line and it is the B and H army members who are calling to you who are also on their defence line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the distance between the two lines was --

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was some 50 to 70 metres, I think, so that we could hear well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And so you said, "I am not coming to you. You come to me." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what happened then?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they said, "Here we come." And they came closer, some 20 or 30 metres, there were some trees there, and I think they were behind a trailer, and again he called, "Dugonja, here we come from the dugouts." And then I came from the dugout and I shouted to my combatants, "Don't fire because these are my neighbours." So that's how it was. Two of them came and I recognised them. "Good morning." "Good morning." "Do sit down." A couple of minutes later, two more turned up. They were in uniforms with rifles in their hands, and that was how it was. And then I made some coffee and I also had some plum brandy and there was also some bacon because that winter I had slaughtered a pig. So we sat down and talked over the coffee, since before, like friends. So they started going back and said, "Please, tell them not to fire at us." And I turned to my combatants and said, "Fellows, don't you fire a bullet." And so they went back. And we later on agreed that we did not have really to fire at one another because we did not need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. You mentioned that you told your guys not to fire. But what were you doing there? Did you have a rank or something?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I commanded a platoon and I covered -- I was responsible for ten dugouts and looked after what they needed, whether some would need food or firewood or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was approximately the length of these ten dugouts that you protected?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: You mean in metres? Well, I don't know exactly. Two or three hundred metres. I wouldn't really know. Ten dugouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that area was under you, you were responsible for it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was under my control, and, of course, I had another commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I realise that. Now, let us go back to this event. So now, after your neighbours, those Muslims, had a cup of coffee with you, had some bacon and had a glass or two of plum brandy, they simply went back to their lines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did anyone fire a shot at them or anything?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Nobody fired at them because we simply didn't feel like having a war on our hands. We didn't feel like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What time was it about?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was about 10.00, I think, and I think we sat for about two hours there, until about noon, and then they went back. A very short while later, my commander arrived, who said, "Were there Muslims here?" And I said, "Yes, there were." And he said, "Why?" And I said, "Well, you know." "And you invited them?" "Yes, I did." And there was also my neighbour in the trench, my next-door neighbour, Miljenko Perkovic. "Miljenko, were you there too?" "Yes, I was." So they came the second shift and told us, "You come with me." So we went with him and he questioned us again and took notes and made some records and told us, "Go home and we shall see what will happen." So I went back home, took a bath, and the sun had set, I think it was dark already, and I fell asleep. At 1.00 in the morning, I heard some bangs on the door. My wife got up and then called to me and said, "It's the Military Police." And they were very angry, very angry at the time. And they said, "Dugonja, here are the orders signed by Mance. Seven days in --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter could not hear.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: "Well," I said, "I won't go. I mean, it's night-time." "No, you must come." There were two of them -- "These are the orders. You must come with us" -- whom I knew. They were our guys. And they said, "Dugonja --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. You said the Military Police came. That is why I interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter could not hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That they brought an order. Was it in writing? Was the order in writing?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not see that, but I heard "seven days of imprisonment." And I resisted. I said, "I don't want to go. Wait," I said. "In the morning. We'll go in the morning. No problem." "No, no, you must come straight-away." So I got ready and my neighbour Miljenko Perkovic was already in the car waiting and we headed straight for the gaol. So they put us together to see what had we done, and I was really crying with rage. Why do we need it? Why did we need any written orders? Nobody fired, nobody was killed, nobody was injured, so -- but -- well ... That day we spent in the cell, lunch, supper --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. You said that the Military Police took you to prison. What prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Kaonik, Kaonik. There were no other prisons over there, at least I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And they turned you over to somebody there. Who did they --

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Military Police. Those who also worked at Kaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who also worked there as guards?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were guards there. Also our guys, I mean, and I knew them, and to each his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you and your neighbour Perkovic, you were put in a cell?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we were in a cell together, and that day, we, I think, went out two or three times. I think it was two or three times that we were let out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. I shall interrupt you once again but we shall come back to this point. So that morning, when you were brought early in the morning or late in the night, I mean, as you like, you were put in a cell and you spent the day in the cell; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you given anything to eat?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. We went out, five or six of us, and there would be a table there and we would eat there, so we ate something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were taken out to eat.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We ate out in the passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the passage. In the passage of the prison, you mean?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did only you and your neighbour Perkovic eat there, or were there some men who were there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, there were five or six men who would come out and have their meal, and then we would finish our meal and go back to our cells, and others came to eat and it went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what about the hygiene? What about your physiological needs?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was very fine. I mean, we would knock on the door and then the police would come, ask what did we need, see us off to the -- take us to the lavatory and then bring us back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see any incidents in the prison, whether anyone beat anyone or used expletives against someone or anything?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, everything was normal. Everything was all right. Sometimes they would give us a cigarette or two. So everything was normal. I never noticed any incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. So what happened after that first day? What happened on the --

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the next day -- rather, the second night there, the orders were read out in the passage and we were also called out to go and dig the trenches and dugouts. So we came into the passage. There were about 20 of us. We came out two by two. We took the hoes or spades or whatever we laid our hands on. And the first night I went on foot, to dig the trenches, to Strane, which is near Kaonik, near the prison. Not far from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Blazevic, you said that somebody in the corridor was calling out names. Do you know who that was?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Military Police, the guards. They called out names and we came out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who took you from Kaonik to Strane where you then dug the trenches?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Military Police again. The Military Policemen took us there --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. So the Military Police took you from Kaonik to Strane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were they the same Military Police who served as guards in the prison or some other policemen?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Those who worked in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, I shall repeat the question because it seems that you did not understand me. Earlier you said that Military Policemen served as guards in the prison. Did you know some of them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Well, as a matter of fact, we were taken by the policemen who were in the barracks by the prison, and those who were in the prison, they only called out our names, and we were taken away by other policemen who were next to Kaonik, in their Military Police --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. So you say that the Military Police were in the area of Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Close to it, some 100 metres away, and those Military Policemen took us away and brought us back and we travelled by car. We also went to Prosije and to Kula and we went by car. And the Military Police who were next to the prison, they had their barracks. They were the ones who took us away and brought us back; that is, took us to dig and brought us back from digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Right. So let us come back to that first night when you were digging. You said you walked there to a site called Strane; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far is it from the prison, Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not far, perhaps 10 or 15 minutes on foot. I do not know. We walked there by night and came back. It was not far.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. So you were brought by the Military Police to that location, to Strane, and who was there to receive you?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: The combatants who were there, who were on watch along the line. So they took us and then positioned us there and said where we were to dig and to see where we were to dig and how to dig so as to not make too much noise because we were told that these are our lines and there is the line of the army of B and H, so they would fire on us, and the combatants would then take us away while the fire lasted, they would take us to a shelter so that we would not suffer, and when the fire would stop, they would then take us back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the soldiers, the combatants on the line where you were digging, were taking care -- were seeing to it that you would be safe; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you said that the Military Police called out the names for the work platoon. How many men were roughly in the platoon?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I remember properly, there were about 20 men, or perhaps 20, 25. I wouldn't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who were among those 20, 25 men? You said that you and your neighbour were there. Who else was there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were Croats and Muslims too. There were also some Serbs who had stayed there and who then joined the unit and who were with the HVO unit until the end. But we all went together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you would finish work, the Military Police would take you back to the barracks?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, and they would either drive us back or we would walk back, depending -- from Strane, we would walk back, and to other places, we would be driven to and from that place by car.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. So you say that you personally, while you were in the Kaonik prison, went to dig in three places: Strane, then Kula, and Prosije?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the labour platoon include Muslims in all these three cases?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did, in all these three cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if there were any incidents during that time? Was anyone wounded or ill-treated or physically harassed while digging?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: While I was there, no, nobody suffered anything. Everybody was perfectly safe, or at least I do not know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Blazevic, how long did you spend in the prison at Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. I spent -- I was sentenced to seven days' imprisonment, but I must say that I did not stay there for seven days, I stayed for five days, because -- and even five days was too much. The Military Police came in one morning and told two of us to go home. He said, "Mance said that you could go back." And we went to the line. And then I asked him, "Why did you condemn us to seven days' imprisonment? What crime had we committed?" "Well," he said, "because we did things on our own initiative. We didn't ask him. Well, how can I ask him? It's all very quick. I had no time to ask you." And I didn't think that this was any of -- that this was any misdemeanour or crime of any kind, and so I forgave him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Blazevic, you said that on the fifth day of your imprisonment, the Military Policemen came and told you that you could go, leave, and they also said that Mance forgave you, that is, Mance let you off these two days, these two additional days?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that's right. And this was -- we liked this. We were very happy that he had done so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So your commander sent you to prison and he amnestied you, that is, he let you off the two days?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, because he had the right to punish us even for as much as 15 days, but he only gave us seven days' imprisonment and then reduced that sentence to two days -- to five days. He let us off for two days, and we were happy, very happy that he did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that -- when you were released from prison, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: We went up to the line straight-away because there was no army, no soldiers. We went to where we were before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, while you were in Kaonik, did you have occasion to see or hear who was the person in charge of the prison there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, of course, I heard from my fellow prisoners that the chief of the prison -- he was pointed out to me, he was Zlatko Aleksovski. I think that was his name. I saw him on one occasion in front of the prison building when we walked around. He was wearing civilian clothes. And I once saw him having a windjammer, sort of camouflage windjammer on. But I saw him very briefly. I don't know the man. He is not from Busovaca. Usually, I know my neighbours, but I did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you say that you do not personally know that man but that one of the prisoners pointed him out to you and said that is the chief of the prison. Yes, I understand. If you saw that man today, do you think you would be able to recognise him?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would be able to recognise him, and if I'm not mistaken, I think that the gentleman sitting over there is that gentleman in question, and as I say, we met in -- I never sat down with him or shook hands with him or had coffee with him, but I know him, and I think it's the man sitting across in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For the record, please indicate that the witness has indicated the individual who was introduced to him, pointed out to him as the chief of the prison, Mr. Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have already said, Mr. Blazevic, but I'll ask you again directly: Do you remember what Zlatko was wearing when you saw him in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I saw him on several occasions. Mostly, he was in civilian clothing. On one occasion, I saw him wearing a sort of windjammer, sort of camouflage windjammer and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps remember, when he was wearing this camouflage jacket, did he have any army insignia on it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any. I don't think he did. I didn't see anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During the time you spent there, did you see what that individual did? Did he issue orders to the guards? Did he communicate with the guards? What did he do there; do you remember? And can you describe it, if so?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say because I never saw him in the prison. I saw him outside, walking around. There was a wood there, and on several occasions, I saw him there. But I don't remember. I don't really know. I don't know. I don't know who issued orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you cannot tell us anything about what he did in the prison?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I cannot say. It was the Military Police which communicated with us. But with this gentleman, the chief, I didn't meet him. I saw him outside on several occasions and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Blazevic, after you were released from prison and after your commander had let you off two days, you went to the line and spent the entire time at the line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You did not go back to Kaonik again?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't. That was my first and last time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know, in the Kaonik facilities, what was located there before the war?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: In the same facility where the Military Police was, well, it was the Serbian army that was there, the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The JNA, you mean?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the JNA. That's correct, the JNA was there. And then our police moved to there and it became a prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Blazevic. Finally, I would like to ask you something that you mentioned at the beginning of your testimony. You have a large family, and you said that you had some casualties. Who, in fact -- what happened to your immediate family? Were you personally ever wounded?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I was never wounded. I said that my three sons were wounded. One is a 60 per cent invalid, the other is a 30 per cent invalid, and the third was just hit in the hand and my brother was killed. Six children remain. My 17-year-old son was killed when he went to dinner and my wife's brother was killed. So I paid dearly in this war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The Defence rests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, it might be the right time for a break. You probably have questions to put to the witness, but how about having the break now, and then you can proceed. Does that suit you? Fine. We are going to have a 20-minute break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, Mr. Niemann is going to put a few questions to you. Mr. Niemann, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Blazevic.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, you were speaking of the location of --

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, do you think we could have that screen put down? It's standing between the witness and myself, and I think it would be easier if it could be just laid down. Just push the top down. That would be fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's better, Mr. Blazevic. We can see each other now. You were speaking, in your evidence, about the locality of the trenches in the vicinity of your house when they were first set up. Do you remember speaking about that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you tell me when the first trenches were put there by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? When did that first happen?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It happened in January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How long had you --

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: And a little before that. I apologise. A little before that, sometime before that, in the second half of 1992, some six months earlier, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: They were there, would it be fair to say, in at least October of 1992? They had already been dug by that stage?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. That was how it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it manned by units of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina from October 1992 up until, say, January of 1993? Were there men there all the time, armed?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Only Muslims, members of the BH, they dug the trenches along the hills around Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it from October until January of 1993, so from October 1992 until January of 1993, there was no firing of guns or anything at you during that period. It was only after January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you'd agree with me, from your general knowledge, that during the period October or, perhaps, even earlier, 1992 up until January 1993 at least, there was a war going on between the Muslims and the Serbs and the Croats at that stage, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was in Croatia, whereas, where we were, there was still no conflict. There was no shooting yet. It was tense, but no shooting. We thought that this would be avoided, that it wouldn't happen in Bosnia, because there had never been a conflict between the Muslims and Croats there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not talking about that conflict. I'm talking about the conflict between, let's say, the JNA in Bosnia in 1992 and the Croats and the Muslims. That was happening in 1992, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. More or less, that was what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Sarajevo, at least, was under siege at that time?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The JNA were carrying out military activity in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Indeed, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, assisted by the HVO, were defending themselves against the JNA in relation to --

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: -- attacks taking place in Bosnia. During this period, when they first erected the trenches, up until January, there was never any suggestion that they were going to be directed towards you at that stage, because there was a war going on between the JNA and the Muslims; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is at least what they said, and they personally told me that it was not against the Croats, but against the Chetniks. But where are the Chetniks? They are 100 kilometres away, and they said, "Well, that's what it is." If I remember correctly, I went to the president of the municipality of Busovaca, Mr. Zoran Maric, I believe, and I said, "Gentlemen, do something, because there will be trouble." He just told me, "It's not your affair. You have your own business to attend to. Nothing will happen." I left, but I was right, in fact, and that is an instance where I personally spoke up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, you weren't right to start with, because nothing had happened right from six months or so after they dug the trenches. But what you are saying is that you ultimately were right, because it was after January when the trenches were used in an attack upon your area?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Were these trenches manned by the Muslims for all of that period, from, say, October of 1992 right up until January? Were they there all that time, or did they just dig them, go away, and then come back in January?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure. I only know when my children attended the livestock, that they were digging trenches, and they took children away. Now, whether they were digging all the time, I don't know. I didn't move up around those hills. I didn't dare, because woods are woods, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Right up until January, in the period leading up until January, did anyone actually fire at your house, anyone from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Did they actually fire at your house during that period, right up until January 1993?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I don't actually remember. I don't know that there was any shooting, but there was tension. It was tense, but no shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But up until when the fighting started in January 1993, did you feel safe enough to walk around your property? Were you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't safe walking around along the hills where they were trench digging. I was afraid of walking over the hills, so I didn't dare.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: During that period, from October 1992 right through to January 1993, was anyone, either your immediate family or anyone nearby, neighbours, shot or injured with rifle fire from this area that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. There was no shooting up until then. Until our two soldiers were killed at Kacuni, there was no shooting up until then, but there was tension, as I say. Quite simply, the situation was tense, and you could see that there would be trouble ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When the fighting did begin in January of 1993, was that the time when you built trenches on your own property?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Our soldier who was killed up there, up until then, we did not have a single trench, nor was there any digging until that shooting had taken place. Then there was fighting between the natural shelters, but there were no trenches until that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When was the soldier shot, what date? Can you remember? I know it's a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: It was a Sunday. It was 12.00, 1.00 p.m. I don't quite remember. It was the 25th or 26th of January, I believe.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually move into Busovaca, into the town, the city of Busovaca itself, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No. It did not enter the town of Busovaca. Before our two soldiers were killed, in fact, from Busovaca, they passed by my house, took cattle past my house towards the hills where there were Muslims. The women and children took the cattle that way. I was personally able to notice that, to notice that we would be attacked, but until then, it did not enter Busovaca. Quite simply, they were in the hills, and it is my personal opinion, I sort of imagined them -- I sort of thought they would attack in the next two days and storm Busovaca, and that's what happened. A young man was killed then. Then we were attacked in an organised fashion in three lines. I remember how it happened. When my children shouted, one of my uncle's children, he was crying, and he said, "Here they are. They are all coming in white." By the road, there was a truck and trailer, and they said, "Hello there." It was sort of a freestyle talking. "This is the Jihad war. This is Islam."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm just interested in you telling me what part the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina actually invaded and what part they occupied in Busovaca? That's the part I would like you to tell me, if you could. You don't have to go off into other details. Just tell me that.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, by Busovaca, there was an encirclement. They attacked, and each time they succeeded in repelling our soldiers, driving them out, sometimes 500 metres to one kilometre. Then we would entrench again, so that we were an encirclement. Luckily, in Busovaca, there was this encirclement. There was one exit towards Sevischa (phoen) down towards Bugojno and Kupres. So we were able to exit that way, and some people did get out through there. But luckily, that is to say, the Muslims cut across this line, and so there was no where else we could go. We were in sort of a pot, and that is where we stayed, and we had no where to escape to. I know that they had taken control of part of Prosije and Kula, so they took control of these places.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The places where they took control, by and large, most of them were actually areas which were mainly Muslim towns. That's right, isn't it? There, up in the hills -- well, not necessarily the hills, but they were mainly Muslim towns?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No. There was nobody's towns there. There were woods and fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Well, an area where a majority of Muslims lived?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember that they took a village called Sokolic where they were inhabited by both Muslims and Croats, but the Croats had withdrawn towards the town, because they knew they couldn't stay there, and they took control of that. There was Putis and there was Kiseljak with a mixed population, but mostly Muslim villages, though, and that's what they took.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You then spoke of trenches being built up on your property or in the vicinity of your property before you were taken off to Kaonik yourself. When they arrived, when those prisoners arrived, I think you said that some of them were Croats and some were prisoners; is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, the Croats could have been from the home guard, couldn't they? They could have been people who were gathered up and brought up to big trenches?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: They were Croats, yes, that's right, those who were not able-bodied men for army service, those who were slightly older and were able to dig, to cut wood, and so on. It was mostly those people, whereas the military-able men went up to the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: That's right. These people were basically civilians but had been put into labour units to perform the sort of work that involved digging trenches around your place?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The prisoners that you saw, they were the Muslims from Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When it came to bringing these people there, these prisoners, particularly, from Kaonik, were you able to see whether the Military Police stayed with the prisoners, as opposed to the volunteers or the able-bodied men who were brought there, the Croats who were brought there? Were you able to see whether the Military Police stayed with the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No. The Military Police would only bring the prisoners, and they would go back to the barracks. The soldiers who were there, that is, the guards on the line there, watched them, and the Military Police returned to their unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it that when it came to digging trenches on your property, at that time, things had become quite dangerous by then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think you said that it became unsafe at that time. Was it unsafe for you to actually leave your house and just walk around the fields around your house?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I have to explain certain things. I think you did not quite understand what I was saying. My property is on the hill, a little bit further away way, some three or four kilometres away. Up there, I had some land where my cattle grazed, and there, up in the hills, the Muslims were digging trenches. By my house, that is where the Muslims came to dig trenches. Up there, where they were digging, I did not dare go there, nor did I ever go, because they had already taken the hills around Busovaca. You have to realise that there must have been three or four, and I don't really remember, perhaps even more, from the place where I had my property. That is where the Muslims were digging before the conflict erupted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You're quite right. I didn't understand that. At the land where you had for grazing your cattle, that's where the trenches were dug, not only by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also by the HVO and the Muslim prisoners, so both of them were built together. Have I got it right now or not?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell me, firstly, where were the trenches dug by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Were they dug at your house or up in the hills?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Up in the hills where I have land. I told you, some three, four, perhaps, five kilometres up there, I have land. It cannot be worked with machinery, so it was used for grazing. Up there, only the Muslims dug their trenches. Then I went to notify the president of the municipality and told him, "Listen, this is not good, because it is my field where they were digging, and they are asking no one."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Fine. Tell me, when it came to the trenches being dug by the prisoners from Kaonik and by the home guard, where was that done? Was that done near your house or, again, up in the hills near the Muslim trenches?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Then the Muslims and Croats came to help us by my house. That was this very narrow, very small circle which we had to defend, because we could not take a larger area, as we were very few. So they came to work at my house, and those were also prisoners who helped us to dig trenches there by my house, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The trenches which were later built by the Muslim prisoners from Kaonik was near your house, and did it face fresh trenches that had been dug by the Muslims near your house?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you can't see that, sir, if that was far away from my house. There are woods and hills, and you can't see that. You can see up to 100 metres, but those hills are high. You can't see it because there are woods and hills. It was all masked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the trenches that were dug -- just excuse me. Just listen to my question. I'm not asking you about trenches that were dug in October of 1992. I'm now moving forward to the trenches that were dug in 1993. You spoke of Muslim prisoners and Croat home guards digging those trenches, and you now say that that was near your house. Are you saying that, by this stage, the Muslim forces had moved down close to your house?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, no, they had not moved. Well, somewhere up in the hills where my unit was, they did, perhaps, a few metres or so. I don't know. But as regards my house and the Muslim house, you could not see it, because the trenches were dug by night, at night-time, so you could not see it. When the day would come, you could see, of course, where the fire was made. When they talked, you could hear them because it was so close. But, otherwise, they worked at night, so you couldn't see anything. I don't know, really, what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: We are having difficulty communicating. I agree. Tell me, the trenches that were built near your house, presumably, faced the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or did they face nothing? Were they dug there for no particular military reason?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Tell me, where was the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina located relative to the trenches that were built near your house?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Everywhere around where our dugouts were, and 100, 150, or, perhaps, 200 metres away, depending on the terrain, was where the Muslims were, all around it. Around my house was, perhaps, no-man's land, and perhaps not more than 50 or 70 metres away, as the crow flies, was theirs, so that we could really talk. I mean, once we raised our voices a little, we could perfectly communicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When they built trenches next to your house, they were, in fact, building trenches on the front line?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Therefore, the trenches that had been built up in the hills in October 1992 were not the trenches that were then being used in an attack on your place?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you. I have to explain this. The trenches or the dugouts were not in a straight line, because, of course, it depended on the terrain. Where we had our property up in the hills, yes, it's true that the Muslims had their trenches. But down there, they were further away from my house, but they were next to each other. I mean, they weren't very close. Of course, naturally, the Muslim trenches were dug first, and then our army came as near as they could, and then they dug trenches also there. I don't really see why you don't think it all fits in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You shouldn't think that I don't think that it all fits in. I'm merely asking you questions, and I'm trying to ascertain the relationship between the trenches that were dug in October 1992 and the trenches that were dug in 1993. It's not a case of me not thinking they don't fit in. I'm asking to you tell me how they do fit in.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Those trenches which they dug in '92 must have been -- and it was proved also for the heavy artillery, sir, because from the altitude, from up there, they could cover the valley. The infantry was in front, as far as they could move, depending on the configuration on the ground. That is where they dug separate trenches. There were two or three lines, because sometimes they advanced or went back, depending on the attack. What I'm trying to say is that the trenches dug in '92 were there to house the artillery, guns, cannons, and what not. I don't know what they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever see firing, of either artillery or anything else, taking place personally? Did you personally see any firing from the trenches that were built in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Not once, but several times. Naturally, they fired, because that is where they deployed their artillery. Across from my property, at the other end, they had something strong, I think a tank or something, but an older tank. From there, they fired at my house, because it's all been pierced. It's now like a sieve.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But a tank, for example, wouldn't have been in a trench, I take it. That's something which would have been brought in.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: That tank was at another vantage point, a protected one. I don't know. I wasn't there. But a tank, an old one or something, I think it was 100 millimetres. That is from that attack. Of course it was protected. You couldn't see it, really. How did they do it? I don't know. But that is where fire came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from knowing that something was being fired from up in the hills, you wouldn't know precisely where it was?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do not know exactly, that is true, but they did fire from some rather powerful weapons because the shells had completely pierced my house, I mean, went right through it, so it must have been some rather powerful weapon. The shells simply went through my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you went to the Kaonik prison, when you were taken there in the middle of the night, what part of the prison were you put into? Were you put into the cells or were you put into a big hangar?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the cell where the JNA had been accommodated. That was the first time I came there. And by the road, right at the entrance which was protected by wire, there was a building where the unit of the Military Police was accommodated, and right up to it, there were some trees and there was a hangar and there were cells, and that is where they were put up, and I was in a cell, yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you remember what cell number you were in?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Do you know of any other prisoners who had been in the HVO who were in those cells at the time when you were there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Why, yes, I did. There were some neighbours. Why, what for, what offence they had committed, I don't really know. We were in no conditions to talk. With me there was this neighbour of mine, and we went together to dig trenches and would come back together, and I spent five days there and then they released me. And that's all I know. About the rest, I know nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But this was the neighbour that was taken to prison with you. I'm talking about other people who were there at the prison when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: They were in other cells. I was with my neighbour in one cell. And in others, I don't know. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you hear of a prisoner called Miroslav Bralo otherwise known as Cicko?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Is it your evidence that you have no idea who else was kept in the other cells?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were people, I don't know how many of them. There were Muslims and Serbs and Croats. All of them were there. But why they were there, I really don't know, and I can't tell you what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you say there was -- apart from the Muslims, that there were Serbs and Croats. How many Serbs were there and did you know them by name?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I know a couple of Serbs and others. There were two brothers, as far as I remember, and they went back to the unit, to the HVO. Miroslav Bilic, Miro Bilic; they were Serbs. One of them was even the commander of the 2nd Battalion. And they're still there. They're businessmen now, I think. They are into wholesale trade and they still live there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Apart from the Bilic brothers, who you say were Serbs, who else was there who were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. There are still Serbs there who stayed behind. But I don't really remember. It was night-time. You went out at night and came back at night, so I can't tell you what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm talking about the prisoners in the cellblock in which you were in. I'm asking you, in the cellblock in which you were in, were there Muslims, Croats, and Serbs? And that's what I'm specifically asking you about.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Correct, yes, true. Where I was, in cells -- I mean, there were Serbs and Muslims and Croats, we were all together, and we all went to dig together.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apart from the Bilic brothers who were in the cells with you, who you say were Serbs, you can't remember anyone else?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. I mean, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, apart from you and your neighbour who were both Croats, I take it, who were the other Croats that were in the cells?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know, it was a long time ago. I really don't remember the names. I cannot say exactly, but they were there. How many, I don't know, but there were some and that is for certain. Whether it was for theft or something else, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: How do you know that they were Croats?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I know who my neighbours were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: But you don't remember who they were now?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I simply do not remember it. I don't really -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that most of the prisoners there were Muslims, weren't they? The majority of them in the cells were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't see that. When we went out digging, there would be two or three of them, but I didn't see. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, what about in other parts of the prison apart from the cellblock where you were? Did you see any other prisoners kept in other parts of Kaonik? Muslims?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I did not see any nor was I aware of the existence or anything like that. It was my first time there. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when the list of prisoners were called out to go trench-digging when you were in Kaonik, who compiled that list? Who made it up?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I haven't the slightest idea. I know the Military Police read them out. But who compiled the lists, I don't know. I can't say I know. I haven't the faintest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, did you hear of the fact, rather than seeing it yourself, but did anyone ever tell you about prisoners being beaten in Kaonik? Did you know that that had happened there?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I don't know. I really don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I think it's your evidence that you never saw any prisoners beaten.

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: That is true. I never saw it. I really don't know. At the time when I was there, nobody laid a finger on anyone nor did anyone touch me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, was your cell locked or open? Did it have a lock on it or was it open?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, sure, locked, locked. The Military Policeman would really lock it. If you wanted to go to the WC, then you knocked. "Yes, please? What do you want?" He would take me to the lavatory, I would finish my business there, he brings me back and locks it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It's possible, do you agree, that people could have been beaten there but you didn't see it or maybe didn't hear it because your door was locked?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, I was behind locked doors, and I did not see or hear anything. But whether anybody was beaten, I simply don't know. Nobody ever laid a finger on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Describe the bed that you slept on. What sort of bed was it?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Boards, just planks or something, but -- nothing but some planks, and we had some newspapers. It was pretty cold then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have mattresses?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, just plain board, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Blankets?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. We had nothing. We only had some newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And was the cell heated?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Nothing, I'm telling you. It was bitterly cold.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have water in the cells?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Could you have a hot shower or a bath?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, nothing. Just a few boards and that was all. There was no light. One could see perhaps through the window a little bit so that we could make out the letters in the newspapers, but that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: When you were taken trench-digging, were you under guard?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The soldiers on the line, they controlled us and said that we had to dig there and not to try to flee because they would shoot if anyone tried to escape. So it was those soldiers who were on the line who guarded us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was this hard work?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what shall I tell you? Well, yes, it was on the hard side because there were rocks there and all sorts of other things, but we had to work. There would be a tin of a kind or something, but it wasn't easy because there was mud and rain and water. But who asks you if you like it or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it cold?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Sure, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have enough warm clothing?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, whatever we happened to be wearing when we were taken there. We had nothing down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you have sufficient breaks, rest breaks?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, to smoke a cigarette, five minutes, ten minutes, fifteen. For a chat or so, but we mostly dug.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was it dangerous?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Very. Very dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Why was it dangerous?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: 'Cause we were not allowed to talk. We were not to do anything. We had to use the pick, to do it very quietly because we were very close to the lines and we would hear a burst of fire. Sometimes people got killed. At the time when I was in the prison, nobody -- there were no casualties, fortunately. We all returned alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any stories of people that were taken out for trench-digging who were beaten?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I did not hear that anyone had been beaten but I heard that a Muslim had been killed, allegedly, from the opposite direction. He was a neighbour of mine and I personally knew him.
