I think his name was Musafer Ibrilic called Cakara. I heard that he had been killed on the line. But from what I had heard, it was a stray bullet from the opposite direction, and I know that he had been killed. I don't know about others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I take it that when you said in your evidence that five days was too much in Kaonik for you, what you meant by that was that these conditions where you had no bedding, you didn't have adequate facilities in order to wash yourself, where you were exposed to danger, doing hard work trench-digging where you could have been shot or killed, all of these things you put together in your mind and said "This is really far too much" for the small thing that you had done wrong?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the worst thing was, when my own people imprisoned me, people that I liked, we're all one, that they should -- that had I been shut up by the BH army, the Muslims, I wouldn't have minded. If they put me away, I wouldn't mind. But this was done by my own people and I even could have been killed. I dug like an ox, like a horse. My circulation is poor to this day in my knees because it was so cold, and I cursed my commander, I told him of all these things, but I had to stick it out. What could I do? And that is the whole truth. It's terrible, but it's true. Before the war, my hair was dark, but I'm like -- I'm grey now, as white as a sheet because I was spent. I experienced some terrible things during the war. And it's a marvel that I'm sane today. I don't think you could even make a film of all the terrible things that I had experienced. But a man can survive more than a horse, stronger than a horse, and I somehow survived, and those are the things that I experienced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Just bear with me a moment. I'll just see if I have any more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, do you want to ask further questions of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Perhaps two or three questions, nothing more, for clarification purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, you answered the question put to you by my learned friend the Prosecutor that you had not seen anybody beaten or physically mistreated in the Kaonik prison camp or on the lines; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I didn't see any of that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps see, when you were in the working group, the labour group, the labour unit with other prisoners, did you see anybody have any -- was bloody perhaps or had any injuries or had black eyes or bruises or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see anything of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Blazevic, that in the cell in which you were locked, that there was no heating. Did you notice in the building, whether in the hall there was a stove of any kind?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice anything. I know that I was cold. I froze to death there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I have one more question for you because I don't think that it was recorded. When you dug, up at the lines, were you given any food, and if so, what were you given?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Well, fish tins, a piece of bread -- tins of fish, a piece of bread, and that's it. Nothing more. We were fairly hungry, and that's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Only one question, Mr. Blazevic. At that time, did you ever see soldiers wearing uniforms with the HV insignia on them, the HV, the Croatian army insignia on them?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see that. I know the HVO -- it was the HVO, but no other army. I did not see any other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Blazevic, do you feel more rested? More at ease now?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: I feel a little better now. It's a little easier for me now, but not much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I can imagine. I do have a few questions to put to you. You stated that you and another colleague of yours were detained in the same cell. Were there other people in that very same cell, or were there only the two of you?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Just the two of us, myself and my neighbour. We were in the cell. Just the two of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I see. Did you get to know other people who happened to be in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: No. I could not have because I didn't have occasion to. We were together in a cell, we went out digging at night, we were taken back to our cell, so you didn't have time or there were not the circumstances for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I believe that you stated that you had heard other people telling prisoners that Mr. Aleksovski was the director of the prison. Did I get you right?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: This was told me by my neighbour, Miljenko Perkovic. He said, when we went outside, "This is the chief of the prison or head of the prison." I had never seen him up until then because he doesn't live in Busovaca. And then I saw him and that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, when you said that you had had other people tell prisoners -- actually, you heard your colleague being told that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLAZAN BLAZEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from my neighbour. And when we went trench-digging, he said, "The man outside wearing civilian clothing is the chief of the prison." That's all. I didn't know the man myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Fine. Well, I don't think that the Judges have other questions for you. I hope that you will go home safely. Thank you very much for coming to testify here in this case. Thank you very much, sir. You may be released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you all too. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you may proceed. It's your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence, in its response, as a fact witness, it has only envisaged to call Mr. Blazevic. The Defence felt that at this point in time, we would be discussing our proposal for including testimony from the Blaskic trial, and that is why, for today, we have just called this one witness. For tomorrow, we have envisaged other witnesses testifying to the character of the accused. So if the Trial Chamber agrees, the Defence would like to propose that a decision be taken, a ruling be made, with regard to the Defence request with regard to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic suggests that we discuss the evidence which you wish to have tendered as evidence; is that right? At any rate, I believe that the Chamber has already ruled on this, even though it was an oral ruling, so the matter is settled at any rate. I'm quite willing to see what Mr. Niemann has to say with respect to this. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Niemann, because in terms of our ruling -- you only asked for the evidence coming from the Blaskic case to be admitted as evidence in our case. I was about to ask the registrar to give a single number for the exhibit -- I think we are dealing with the statement by Admiral Domazet, we are dealing with the documents which were used during his testimony, and we are also dealing with the video that he also introduced through his testimony, so they will be all marked as one exhibit, though we have to deal with three different pieces. This was an oral ruling which I issued, put to you this morning, so we are going to ask the registrar to give a single exhibit number, but we are going to issue a decision in writing, and this will be reasoned and you will see why we came to such a decision. But you made a specific proposal. Let me hear what Mr. Niemann has to say on this. Do you have anything to say, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would have said a great deal, but seeing as Your Honours have made your ruling, I don't think there is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Niemann, yes. I'm only speaking as to the suggestion made by Mr. Mikulicic, because as to the merits, we have already ruled. It's only whether -- you can also appeal the decision, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: There's nothing I can say in the face of Your Honours' ruling. Your Honours have made your ruling and I'm content with that, and we move on, so far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, did you want to intervene?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, if I may? I proposed that this tendering of evidence of General Domazet's testimony in the Blaskic case be done, and with regard to that, you have already given us a ruling. But I don't know how the Trial Chamber feels -- and this is something that the Defence would like to put forward -- that here, in the Trial Chamber, we look at the videotape of that testimony, and so in that way, we could all have direct knowledge of that testimony as well as all the other elements which went as part and parcel of the testimony and which you suggested be one exhibit, three pieces. That was my question. And I would like to have an answer in that direction and to hear your stand on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I would like to address Your Honours on that point, if I may? Yes. I don't see why it's necessary, Your Honours, why we have to all sit here and watch a videotape or read the transcript, have it read out, or whatever. My understanding was that there was an application to have this admitted as an exhibit in the proceedings that Your Honours could consider along with all the other exhibits Your Honours have, and I think it should be kept that way. I don't think there is any necessity for it to be played. It's a matter for Your Honours to consider when you come to consider the totality of the evidence. So, Your Honours, the Prosecution is opposed to it being played or read out or whatever is proposed. Your Honours made a ruling that it be tendered, and that's the stage it's at at the moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, to be more specific, and I'm going to ask Mr. Marc Dubuisson to tell us what this exhibit number, the single exhibit number will be for all these documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be D35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: To answer the question raised by Mr. Mikulicic, let me tell you this: We have ruled that this public document be tendered, be admitted as evidence, which is now D35. Both parties and the Chamber may, whenever they so wish, either read the statement by this witness, look again at the video clip, look again at all of these documents. Our ruling did not aim at having the exhibit be displaced because we are talking about public documents, public records, and the Tribunal is aware of them. To make things easier, we already know that we are dealing with the Exhibit D35, which means that either the Defence or the Prosecution may turn to the registry and ask for copies of all these records. We did not have in mind that the transcript should be read or that the video cassette should be viewed because we have the documents anyway and, you know, we are working by half days, and it would take at least two full days to either look at the transcript or watch the video cassette. Since we are talking about public records, you have full access to them, and anybody interested in such documents may feel free to access the documents. So we are dealing with something else altogether. It would be different if we were to have the physical presence of Admiral Domazet, that would be totally different, but the basis and the foundation for our ruling has been given, everything has been tendered into this case as evidence, so all of Admiral Domazet's evidence has now become our evidence. You have the documents, they have been tendered into evidence, they are available to you, and there is no need for us to see all this again. I think it may be in the interests of the Chamber to raise another question, and let us avail ourselves of this opportunity to convene a short Status Conference in closed session. I am now turning to the technical booth. I think we should move into closed session for a short Status Conference. Thank you. Can we moved into closed session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: following the Status Conference, to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 20th day of October, 1998, at 9.00 a.m.
